extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and readers studying species, hybridisation, and variation (readers of The Origin of Species)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for distinguishing species from varieties and for understanding/assessing hybrid fertility, causes of sterility, and resemblance patterns in crosses and grafting. Emphasises empirical tests (crossing, reciprocal crosses, grafting) and interpretation of their outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility of first crosses and hybrids as a diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: First crosses between distinct species, and the hybrids produced from them, are very generally, but not universally, sterile; fertility ranges from zero to perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of sterility is variable among species and individuals, is susceptible to favourable and unfavourable conditions, and can differ between a first cross and the hybrids produced from it. Two careful observers may reach opposite conclusions using this test. Fertility therefore can be used as a criterion but is not absolute; interpret results in light of variability, environmental effects, and experimental replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic affinity partly predicts crossing facility
rubrics_metrics.description: The facility of making first crosses is largely governed by systematic affinity (resemblance in structure and constitution), but the correspondence is not strict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrids have not been raised between species ranked in distinct families, and closely allied species often unite readily; however, many counterexamples exist (e.g., Dianthus vs Silene, varying genera within same family, Nicotiana exceptions). Do not rely solely on taxonomic proximity; test empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal crosses can differ widely in result
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal crosses (A♂×B♀ vs B♂×A♀) often show marked differences in ease of fertilisation and in hybrid fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large differences in reciprocal crosses indicate reproductive differences confined to the sexual/reproductive system rather than whole-organism affinity. Example: Mirabilis jalappa fertilised by M. longiflora succeeds, but the reciprocal attempt repeatedly failed. Record and compare reciprocal crosses when assessing crossing capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility independent of external resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: The sterility of hybrids is not related to the degree in which they externally resemble either parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrids that closely resemble one parent may nonetheless be extremely sterile. External similarity should not be taken as proxy for reproductive compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterility is incidental, not a specially endowed quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterility of first crosses and of hybrids is probably incidental on unknown differences (chiefly in reproductive systems), not an adaptation specially endowed to prevent blending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sterility varies in degree, between individuals, and across reciprocal crosses, it is more plausible that sterility results from incompatibilities in reproductive systems than from a purposeful protective endowment. Use parsimony when interpreting sterility as an evolutionary function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical barriers to fertilisation (mechanical/pollen‑stigma incompatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some crosses a physical impossibility prevents the male element reaching the ovule (e.g., pistil too long); or pollen-tubes may protrude but fail to penetrate the stigmatic surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a cross fails, examine floral morphology and pollen–stigma interactions to distinguish mechanical or cellular refusal from later-acting causes. Document pollen‑tube behaviour where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of male element to induce embryo development
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when male and female elements meet, the male element may be incapable of causing an embryo to be developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cellular/genetic incompatibilities beyond mere physical contact; refer to experimental cases (e.g., Thuret’s Fuci) to infer gametic incompatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early embryo death as a common cause of sterility in first crosses
rubrics_metrics.description: An embryo may be developed and then perish at an early period, which is a frequent cause of sterility in first crosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate embryonic development stages when crosses fail; anecdotal evidence (Mr. Hewitt on gallinaceous birds) suggests early death is important. Distinguish pre‑ and post‑implantation/seed developmental failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterility of hybrids due to disturbed organisation from compounded structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrids have their organisation disturbed by being compounded of two different structures, which affects the reproductive system and often causes sterility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret hybrid sterility as arising from developmental disturbance of coordination among organs; hybrids that can breed inter se transmit the compound organisation, so sterility patterns may persist across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between grafting capacity and crossing capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity for grafting follows a rude degree of parallelism with crossing: both are limited to some extent by systematic affinity but exceptions occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grafting observations as supplementary evidence of physiological affinity but not as definitive proof. Examples: pear grafted readily on quince (different genus) but less readily on apple (same genus); variability among varieties in graft‑take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of unnatural conditions/domestication on reproductive systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing organisms from natural conditions commonly affects their reproductive systems and can induce sterility; domestication can render some species sterile or increase variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing fertility, control for environmental/maintenance conditions and history of domestication. Note that domestication may both decrease and increase fertility and variability in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility of varieties usually high but not decisive for species status
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties generally cross with facility and yield fertile offspring, but notable exceptions exist; fertility alone cannot be taken as a fundamental distinction between species and varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware circular reasoning: if an infertile 'variety' is discovered, it will often be reclassified as species. Empirical counterexamples (Gärtner’s maize, Verbascum colour varieties, tobacco varieties) show fertility exceptions. Combine fertility evidence with other characters and history of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of mongrels (variety crosses) and hybrids (species crosses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mongrels are more variable than hybrids in the first generation; both can show extensive variability in later generations, but mongrels often show greater early variability and reversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generational patterns of variability as diagnostic information: first-generation variability greater in mongrels suggests recent variability in parental lines; hybrids often show pronounced variability in subsequent generations due to disturbed reproductive systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepotency and patterns of resemblance in crosses
rubrics_metrics.description: One parent often has a prepotent power of impressing its likeness on offspring; prepotency can be sex‑linked and may cause hybrids or mongrels to resemble one parent more strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess parentage effects and sex-specific transmission (e.g., ass over horse), and record whether prepotency runs more strongly in one sex. Exceptional resemblances (monstrous characters) can appear and affect interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcrossing increases vigour; prolonged close inbreeding induces weakness/sterility
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight crosses between distinct strains (outcrossing) generally give vigour and fertility to offspring; close interbreeding continued for generations tends to cause weakness and sterility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fertility and vigour, account for breeding history: recent outcrossing often masks underlying incompatibilities, while long-term inbreeding can produce sterility unrelated to species differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental replication and careful manipulation required for fertility tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Fertility outcomes are innately variable and sensitive to experimental conditions and individual constitution; thorough and replicated crossing experiments (including reciprocal crosses) are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because two careful experimentalists can disagree using fertility as a test, ensure multiple reciprocal attempts, controlled conditions, and examination of developmental stages (pollen tubes, embryos) before drawing taxonomic conclusions.
